title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #1
description: Full-length 53-question simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes).

questions.prompt: A fintech company processes loan applications through a fixed sequence: extract applicant data from a PDF form, run it through a credit-scoring API call, and generate a standardized approval/denial letter. The steps and their order never change; only the input data varies. Which approach best fits building this pipeline?

options.text: A single autonomous agent given a broad toolset (file access, web search, code execution) and instructed to 'process the loan application end to end,' letting it improvise the extraction, scoring, and letter-drafting steps itself on every run.
A workflow that chains a fixed sequence of LLM calls and deterministic code, orchestrated by code you control, since the sequence and branching logic are already known.

A manager agent that spawns a brand-new subagent for every applicant, each one independently re-deciding the extraction, scoring, and letter-generation order from scratch rather than following a fixed sequence.
An MCP server that exposes the entire loan-processing pipeline as a single opaque tool call, so the extraction, scoring, and letter steps happen inside a black box with no visible control structure.

questions.explanation: Because the steps are fixed and known in advance, code-controlled orchestration (a workflow) is more reliable, cheaper, and easier to debug than giving a model open-ended autonomy to redecide the same steps every time. Option A wastes model-driven flexibility on a task with no real decision points and risks skipped or reordered steps. Option C adds delegation complexity for work that has no independent parallel component. Option D just hides the process behind a tool call without answering which control structure should drive execution.

questions.prompt: A team wants to build a multi-step research agent whose control flow includes conditional branches, retries, and explicit state passed between steps, and they want to visualize and control that flow as an explicit graph of nodes and edges rather than an implicit loop. Which kind of framework are they describing?

options.text: A graph-based orchestration framework like LangGraph, which models an agent's or workflow's control flow as an explicit graph of nodes (steps) and edges (transitions), including branches and cycles.
The Claude Agent SDK, because it is the only way to add conditional branching to an agent, since its built-in tools and hooks are themselves implemented as an internal graph of nodes and edges.
The Message Batches API, because it supports large numbers of parallel branches, letting each conditional path in the research agent run as a separate asynchronous batch request with shared state.

A single Messages API call with a much longer, carefully structured system prompt that spells out every conditional branch, retry rule, and piece of state the agent should track as it reasons through the research task.

questions.explanation: Explicit graph-based control flow with nodes, edges, branches, and state is the defining feature of frameworks like LangGraph. The Agent SDK provides a harness and built-in tools, not an explicit graph-authoring abstraction, ruling out option 2. The Batches API is for high-volume asynchronous, independent requests, not control-flow orchestration, ruling out option 3. A longer system prompt cannot reliably encode explicit branching and state logic the way a graph structure does, ruling out option 4.

questions.prompt: A long-running conversation eventually exceeds the context window. What is the appropriate design response?

options.text: Summarise earlier turns into a compact running state and carry that forward
Truncate the oldest turns and continue
Increase the maximum output tokens
Start a new conversation with no history

questions.explanation: Compaction preserves the meaning of earlier exchanges within a much smaller footprint, which is what continuity requires. Blind truncation (B) drops facts silently, the output cap (C) is unrelated, and starting fresh (D) discards the state entirely.

questions.prompt: Which condition warrants a retry with backoff rather than surfacing an error?

options.text: The request contained an invalid parameter
The service returned a rate limit or a transient server error
The model returned an answer you disagree with
The response exceeded the expected length

questions.explanation: Rate limits and transient server errors are the recoverable class. An invalid parameter (A) will fail identically, and disagreement (C) or length (D) are not transport failures

questions.prompt: A batch of 500 jobs finishes. Result row 0 does not match request 0. What should the code do?

options.text: Assume API order equals submit order
Join each result to its request with `custom_id`
Retry the whole batch
Switch to streaming

questions.explanation: Batch results are unordered. `custom_id` is the join key. Retrying or streaming does not fix mapping.

questions.prompt: A request to Claude Opus 5 includes `temperature=0.7`. What happens?

options.text: Sampling works as on older models
The API returns 400 because those sampling parameters are removed
The parameter is ignored and `usage.speed` becomes `fast`
Cost doubles

questions.explanation: 400, not ignore. Unrelated to fast mode billing.

questions.prompt: Claude emits server-side `web_search`. Your app should:

options.text: Run Google yourself and send `tool_result`
Do nothing extra — the result arrives inline
Convert it to stdio MCP
Return HTTP 204

questions.explanation: Server-side: no `tool_result` from you.

questions.prompt: A tool definition sets `"strict": true`. What does this guarantee?

options.text: The tool's side effects are safe
The tool_use `input` will validate exactly against the schema
The tool will always succeed
The response will be streamed

questions.explanation: Strict guarantees *shape*, not safety, success, or streaming.

questions.prompt: A streaming handler receives a `content_block_start` event for a `tool_use` block (carrying the tool `name` and `id`), followed by a long series of `input_json_delta` fragments. At which point can the handler safely parse the accumulated input string and execute the tool?

options.text: As soon as the accumulated string ends with a closing `}`, since that means the JSON object is complete.
After each delta, parsing incrementally so execution starts as early as possible.
Only after the `content_block_stop` event for that block — the accumulated string is not guaranteed to be valid JSON until the block closes.
After the first `message_delta` event, which signals that the tool input has stabilized.

questions.explanation: Tool input arrives as partial JSON fragments and is only guaranteed valid when `content_block_stop` closes the block. A string ending in `}` can still be mid-object (nested braces, trailing fragments to come).

questions.prompt: A developer wants to contribute a pattern from a finished customer engagement — currently embedded in a full application with UI and deploy scripts — to the Claude Cookbook. Which TWO steps are required before the contribution can be accepted? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Extract the reusable pattern into a focused, self-contained example — the Cookbook reviews one pattern, not an application.
Submit the entire application with documentation explaining each component.
Clear the rights check on code carried from the engagement, because a licensing constraint blocks the merge regardless of code quality.
Split the application across several simultaneous pull requests, one per component.
Run a performance benchmark demonstrating the pattern is faster than existing examples.

questions.explanation: The Cookbook reviews one focused, self-contained pattern — a whole application stalls regardless of quality — and engagement-derived code must clear the rights check first, because a licensing constraint blocks the merge before any technical review.

questions.prompt: A Python backend must make many concurrent real-time Claude calls without tying up its application thread; each result goes back to a waiting user. Which pattern fits?

options.text: The Message Batches API, since it accepts many requests in one call.
The AsyncAnthropic async client with non-blocking async/await — requests still return in real time, but the application can handle other work while waiting.
A synchronous loop that issues one call at a time.
Importing the TypeScript SDK's separate async client class into the Python service.

questions.explanation: The Python SDK's AsyncAnthropic client uses non-blocking async/await for real-time concurrency without tying up the thread. Batches is for bulk offline work with no user waiting, and the TypeScript SDK has no separate async client class (its standard client is Promise-based).

questions.prompt: A production integration receives an HTTP 200 response, but the message's stop_reason is "refusal". How should the application handle it?

options.text: Retry the identical request with exponential backoff, since a refusal is transient
Treat the response text as valid output, since the HTTP status indicates success

Raise the refusal to the caller and log it, without silently retrying — the model made a content decision, not a transient error, and the retriable-status classifier will not catch it because the HTTP layer returned 200
Automatically rewrite the prompt and resubmit until the model complies

questions.explanation: A refusal is a 200 at the HTTP layer, so status-based retry classification will not catch it, and it reflects a content decision, not a transient fault. The module's guidance: raise it to the caller and log it; do not silently retry or treat it as valid output.

questions.prompt: A team is placing its engineering work into the systems lifecycle phases for a Claude application. Which TWO activities belong in the deploy phase? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Pinning the full model ID and keeping the prior version available
Deciding that data must be processed in a specific region
Gating promotion on the eval result before a version goes to production
Instrumenting token cost and latency per call in production
Choosing Amazon Bedrock because the customer holds its compliance posture there

questions.explanation: Pinning the full model ID with a retained prior version and gating promotion on the eval result are both deploy decisions. Residency is requirements, the platform choice is design, and production instrumentation is operate.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team wants Claude to analyze a photo of a damaged item alongside a short text instruction in a single request for a returns-processing assistant. What is the correct way to structure this request?

options.text: Images cannot be combined with text in a single Claude request.
Send the image as a separate, unrelated API call and merge the two responses in application code.
Include both an image content block and a text content block in the same message.
Convert the image to a text description manually before calling the API at all.

questions.explanation: Claude's vision capability lets a single message include both image and text content blocks together, so the model reasons over both in one call.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team wants a loan-underwriting assistant to always adopt the same role, tone, and standing behavioral rules on every single call, regardless of what the end user types. Where should this persistent guidance live?

options.text: In a code comment in the backend service, unread by the model.
In the system prompt, which is the dedicated place for persistent, call-spanning instructions.
Repeated at the end of every user message, worded slightly differently each time.
Nowhere — persistent behavior isn't configurable through the API.

questions.explanation: The system prompt is the dedicated parameter for persistent, standing instructions that should apply across every turn, separate from the specific user request.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team must run nightly summarization over 4 million requests/month worth of archived return requests, with no user waiting on any individual result and a deadline of 8 a.m. the next morning. Which integration approach best fits this workload?

options.text: Streaming responses so each summary starts rendering immediately for no one in particular.
Synchronous Messages API calls issued one at a time from the same web-tier process handling live traffic.
One long-lived conversation session that never closes across all records.
The Message Batches API, submitted as an offline overnight job.

questions.explanation: The Message Batches API is designed for large volumes of latency-tolerant, non-interactive requests processed asynchronously — exactly this kind of overnight, no-one-waiting job.

questions.prompt: In application code for a loan-underwriting assistant, a fintech startup's platform engineering team wants to handle an API call failure gracefully instead of letting it crash the request handler. What is the appropriate pattern?

options.text: Remove all timeout and error-handling code to simplify the integration.
Ignore all errors and always show the user a generic success message regardless of outcome.
Let unhandled exceptions from the API client propagate and crash the process.
Wrap the API call in proper error handling (catching exceptions/checking status), logging the failure and applying the right retry or fallback behavior per error type.

questions.explanation: Production integrations should catch and handle API errors explicitly, applying different behavior depending on error type (e.g., backoff for 429/5xx, fail fast for 400/401) rather than letting failures crash the app or go unnoticed.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team wants to safely retry a failed request to the fulfillment service without risking that a downstream action (like sending a notification) happens twice if the original request actually succeeded server-side. What should the integration do?

options.text: Retry as fast and as often as possible with no coordination.
Make retries fully idempotent (or otherwise safe to repeat) so a duplicate call doesn't duplicate side effects.
Never retry any failed request under any circumstances.
Assume side effects never need to be considered when retrying API calls.

questions.explanation: Building retries to be idempotent (or otherwise safe to repeat) is the correct pattern — it lets the application recover from transient failures without risking duplicated side effects.

questions.prompt: A retail company's business requirement states that a checkout-assistance chatbot must respond within 2 seconds even during flash-sale traffic surges of 10x normal volume. Which combination of infrastructure decisions best satisfies this functional requirement?

options.text: Use Claude Opus with extended thinking enabled for the highest-quality responses on every checkout message, and rely on the SDK's default retry logic to smooth over any throughput problems during the traffic surge.

Select a faster, latency-appropriate model tier for short interactive responses, use streaming to reduce perceived latency, and confirm the organization's rate limits/usage tier can absorb the peak throughput (or request an increase in advance).
Switch to the Message Batches API so checkout requests during the flash sale are queued and processed together as an asynchronous batch, trading immediate responses for efficient bulk throughput.

Increase max_tokens substantially so the model has more room to reason through each checkout response, then disable streaming so the client only needs to handle one complete response payload at a time.

questions.explanation: A latency-sensitive, high-throughput interactive workload needs an appropriately fast model, streaming for perceived responsiveness, and pre-planned rate-limit capacity. Option A picks a slower model and has no capacity plan; option C uses the Batches API, which is for latency-tolerant asynchronous jobs, not real-time checkout; option D both increases latency (more max_tokens) and removes the responsiveness benefit of streaming.

questions.prompt: A team is building an internal REST API that wraps calls to the Claude Messages API for use by multiple internal frontends. Which design choice best follows REST API and JSON best practices for this wrapper?

options.text: Return Claude's raw content array unmodified in every response, including internal fields like cache_creation_input_tokens, so frontends can pick out whatever fields they happen to need directly from the upstream shape.

Define a stable, versioned internal response schema (e.g., /v1/chat) that extracts and normalizes the fields frontends actually need, decoupling frontend code from changes in the underlying Claude API response shape.

Encode the entire Claude API request and response payload as a single opaque base64-encoded string in the wrapper's own response body, which simplifies the wrapper's implementation by avoiding field-level parsing.

Require every frontend to send its own Anthropic API key directly to the wrapper in the JSON request body on each call, trusting each frontend team to store and rotate that credential safely on its own.

questions.explanation: A stable, versioned internal schema decouples internal consumers from upstream API changes, a core REST/API design principle. Option A leaks internal implementation details and creates tight coupling. Option C makes the API unusable/unparseable by clients, violating basic JSON API practice. Option D is a serious credential-handling anti-pattern.

questions.prompt: An engineering team wants to standardize a set of custom slash commands, subagents, and hooks across all developers using Claude Code, and ensure that installing an untrusted third-party plugin cannot silently grant it access to run arbitrary shell commands. Which practice best fits this goal?

options.text: Package the shared commands, subagents, and hooks into a version-controlled internal plugin, and review any third-party plugin's declared tools and permissions before installing it, rather than granting broad trust by default.

Ask every developer to manually copy the desired commands, subagents, and hook scripts into their own local settings whenever something changes, treating this ad hoc syncing process as a full substitute for a shared plugin system, since a formal plugin mechanism is unnecessary for a small team.

Install every plugin from the community marketplace using its default "allow all" permission settings, reasoning that Claude Code plugins are sandboxed so they can never access the filesystem or invoke shell commands no matter what permissions or hooks they declare.

Grant every installed plugin full, unrestricted bash access by default on the assumption that any tool-permission restriction would break the plugin's hooks and slash commands, making fine-grained review of third-party plugin permissions unnecessary before installation.

questions.explanation: A version-controlled internal plugin standardizes shared tooling reproducibly, and reviewing third-party plugin permissions before install avoids granting unnecessary trust, directly addressing both goals. Manual copying (B) is unscalable and error-prone, not a real solution. Option C is factually wrong; plugins and hooks can be configured with broad filesystem/shell access, making "allow all" defaults risky. Option D is also false and unnecessarily broad.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to decide between two models for a specific task?

options.text: Choose the one with the better published benchmark scores
Choose the newer model, since it supersedes the older one
Measure both against a representative sample of the real task and its quality bar
Choose the larger model and reduce cost elsewhere

questions.explanation: Model choice is empirical and task-specific, which is what a representative evaluation establishes. Benchmarks (A) may not reflect the task, recency (B) is not a measurement, and defaulting to size (D) decides before evidence.

questions.prompt: You want to measure exactly how many tokens a prompt will cost against `claude-sonnet-5` before sending it. What should you use?

options.text: `tiktoken`
`client.messages.count_tokens(model="claude-sonnet-5", ...)`
`len(text.split())`
The Batch API

questions.explanation: Use Claude's `count_tokens` with that model ID. `tiktoken` is the wrong tokenizer. Word counts are guesses. Batch does not count a draft prompt.

questions.prompt: An agent feature passed testing, but in production some long sessions now return truncated output with `stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded"`. What is happening, and whose job is the fix?

options.text: The model silently dropped the oldest turns and truncated what remained; enabling auto-trimming in the API restores full output.
`max_tokens` is set too low; raising it enlarges the window and removes the truncation.

The growing history and tool results now reach the context window's fixed token ceiling mid-generation; the application must trim or summarize history — the window never expands and the model never silently drops turns.
The requests are being routed to a smaller model variant under load; pinning the full model ID fixes it.

questions.explanation: The context window is a fixed total budget; reaching it mid-generation truncates with `model_context_window_exceeded`. The model never silently drops turns and the window never grows — trimming or summarizing history is the application's job.

questions.prompt: A team is deciding which Claude model tier to use for a new production workload. Which TWO statements reflect the module's guidance? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Sonnet is the balanced default for most production workloads.
Haiku is the most capable tier, built for the most demanding reasoning work.
Move up a tier only when an eval shows the current tier missing the quality bar, and move down to Haiku only when an eval shows the quality drop is acceptable.
Opus is built primarily for speed and cost efficiency on simple tasks.
Model identifiers never change, so there is no need to confirm the lineup in the docs.

questions.explanation: Sonnet is the balanced production default, and tier moves in either direction should be driven by evals. Fable (not Haiku) is the most capable tier, Haiku is built for speed and cost, and the lineup should be confirmed in the docs at build time.

questions.prompt: A developer wants prompt caching to reduce the cost of a high-volume feature. Which TWO conditions must hold for the caching to pay off? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The content before the cache breakpoint must be exactly identical across requests — adding even a single word invalidates the cache and forces a full reprocess
The same prefix must recur within the cache lifetime (five minutes by default, refreshed on each hit), so reads outnumber the premium-priced writes
Cache reads are billed at a premium over base input tokens, so caching only helps on short prompts
The dynamic per-user message should be placed before the cache breakpoint so it is also cached
Caching benefits any prompt regardless of length, so no minimum threshold applies

questions.explanation: The cache matches on an exact prefix, so any change before the breakpoint (even one word) invalidates it, and the saving only lands when the same prefix recurs within the TTL so cheap reads (0.1x) outnumber premium writes (1.25x–2x). Dynamic content before the breakpoint defeats the cache, and prompts below the per-model minimum length see no benefit.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team originally shipped a loan-underwriting assistant using the most capable (and most expensive) model tier for every request 'to be safe.' After running evaluations, they find a faster, cheaper tier meets the quality bar for the vast majority of requests. What should they do?

options.text: Disable evaluation going forward, since the current setup already 'works.'
Right-size the model — move the bulk of traffic to the tier that meets the validated quality bar, reserving the more capable tier only for cases that actually need it.
Switch every request to the fastest, cheapest tier with no further validation of edge cases.
Keep using the most expensive tier everywhere regardless of the evaluation results, since more capability can never hurt.

questions.explanation: Right-sizing — moving the bulk of traffic to the validated, more cost-effective tier while reserving the most capable tier for cases that truly need it — is the correct optimization once evaluation shows it meets the bar.

questions.prompt: A solo developer works across a dozen unrelated repositories and wants Claude Code to always apply one personal preference (e.g., prefer functional-style refactors over imperative ones) in every project, without having to edit each repository. No team members share this preference, and there is no enterprise IT function involved. Where should the developer record this preference so it is loaded automatically in every session?

options.text: Add the preference to the CLAUDE.md file in the root of whichever project they happen to be working in that week, since project-level CLAUDE.md files are loaded for every session in that repository and would need to be duplicated manually into each of the dozen unrelated repos.

Create or edit the user-level CLAUDE.md file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, since Claude Code automatically loads this file into context for every session regardless of which project directory the developer happens to be working in that day.

Ask an organization administrator to add the preference to the enterprise-managed CLAUDE.md policy file, since that file is loaded ahead of all other CLAUDE.md files and is the correct place to record any instruction meant to apply across every repository a developer touches.

Add the preference as a new key inside .claude/settings.local.json for the current project, since settings.local.json is where Claude Code stores free-text memory and behavioral instructions that persist across every session run on that machine.

questions.explanation: The user-level CLAUDE.md is loaded for every Claude Code session regardless of which repo is open, making it the right place for personal, cross-project preferences. Editing a single project's CLAUDE.md only affects that repo. Enterprise-managed CLAUDE.md is for org-wide mandatory policy set by administrators, not a solo developer's personal style preference. settings.local.json holds machine-specific tool/permission configuration, not free-text memory instructions.

questions.prompt: Your service makes a Messages API call and the response carries stop_reason "end_turn" with a tool_use block absent. What does your loop do?

options.text: Treat the turn as complete and return the content to the caller
Execute the last requested tool again
Re-send the request with higher max_tokens
Append an empty tool result and continue the loop

questions.explanation: "end_turn" means the model has finished; "tool_use" is the signal to execute a tool and continue the loop

questions.prompt: A task requires reading through 30 unrelated internal documents and reporting distinct findings from each. What's the strongest justification for using a multi-agent (delegated) design over a single long-running agent?

options.text: It's always cheaper
It keeps the coordinator's context window from filling with reading that has no further relevance to the coordinator's own reasoning
It's required by the API
It avoids all hallucination

questions.explanation: Isolation stops reading debris from filling the coordinator. It is not always cheaper and does not ban hallucinations. The API does not require multi-agent.

questions.prompt: A team keeps a specialized migration checklist in CLAUDE.md. It applies to perhaps one session in twenty, but loads into every session and dilutes the rest of the file. Where should it live?

options.text: A subagent, which automatically inherits all project skills and instructions.
A skill — its name and description load at startup, and the full instructions load only when a request matches the description.
A larger, better-organized CLAUDE.md with headers, since the model reads only the relevant sections.
A pinned first message pasted manually into relevant sessions.

questions.explanation: A skill loads only its name and description at startup and its full instructions only on a matching request — exactly right for one-in-twenty guidance. Subagents do **not** automatically inherit skills, and CLAUDE.md loads whole every session regardless of headers.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team is automating return requests processing for a returns-processing assistant: every case follows the same fixed sequence (extract fields, check policy rules, route exceptions to a human queue, generate a summary), and success is easy to verify. Which architecture is the best fit?

options.text: A long-running agent that must retain memory of every case indefinitely.
A manager agent that delegates every single case to specialized subagents.
A fully autonomous agent that decides each next action for every case.
A deterministic workflow that calls Claude only at defined steps in a known sequence.

questions.explanation: When the sequence and branching are known and fixed and success is easy to verify, a deterministic workflow is the better fit — an open-ended agent would add unnecessary variability the task doesn't need.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team needs to process a large set of independent patient intake forms where each case can be handled without any dependency on the others. Which orchestration pattern is most efficient?

options.text: Force every case through a single shared conversation thread to preserve order.
Route every case through a single subagent one at a time regardless of independence.
Fan the independent cases out to run in parallel, since there is no dependency between them.
Process every case strictly one at a time in a single sequential chain.

questions.explanation: When subtasks are genuinely independent, parallelization (fanning them out concurrently) is the efficient orchestration pattern rather than an unnecessary sequential chain.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team is running a long-lived agent for a loan-underwriting assistant that needs to recall decisions and progress from earlier sessions, not just the current conversation. What capability addresses this?

options.text: Ignoring the need, since agents cannot retain any information across sessions.
Agent memory, which persists relevant state or context across sessions rather than starting from a blank slate each time.
Increasing temperature so the agent 'remembers' more creatively.
A larger max_tokens setting for the current request only.

questions.explanation: Agent memory is the mechanism for persisting relevant state or prior context across sessions, distinct from the current conversation's context window.

questions.prompt: A B2B analytics SaaS platform team is concerned an autonomous agent loop in a report-generation assistant could keep taking actions indefinitely if it never reaches a satisfying stopping condition. What is the appropriate safeguard?

options.text: Remove all stopping logic so the agent can run as long as it likes.
Build in guardrails such as a maximum iteration count or checkpoints, so a runaway loop is bounded rather than open-ended.
Rely solely on the end user to notice and manually kill the process every time.
No safeguard is needed, since agent loops always terminate on their own.

questions.explanation: Bounding an agent loop with guardrails like a maximum iteration count or defined checkpoints is the correct safeguard against runaway or infinite-loop behavior.

questions.prompt: A team's order-processing agent calls two client-side tools per turn. In a batch of 500 failed runs, every `tool_result` block in the logged traces has `is_error: false`, and each Messages API response has `stop_reason: "end_turn"` with HTTP 200. Despite this, roughly 8% of runs produce a final answer that misapplies the discount policy described in the system prompt. Where should the team focus its debugging effort first?

options.text: In the tool-execution code, since a silent tool failure that returns a superficially valid but incorrect result is the most common cause of a final answer misapplying policy, even when the tool_result block itself is marked is_error: false.

In the retry/backoff logic, since transient network errors during that portion of the 500 failed runs are likely corrupting tool inputs in flight before they ever reach the two client-side tools, producing subtly wrong discount values that the model then reports as though they were correct and fully validated.

In the model's reasoning over the retrieved discount policy text and prompt, since the integration layer — API calls, tool execution, and their result blocks — completed successfully and reported no errors, pointing to a generation-quality issue rather than an infrastructure one.

In the API client's request-timeout configuration, since requests that come close to timing out are the leading cause of subtly wrong output, even when the response ultimately completes with HTTP 200 and a normal end_turn stop reason.

questions.explanation: Successful HTTP responses, `stop_reason: "end_turn"", and `is_error: false` on every tool_result together indicate the integration layer (network, auth, tool execution) worked correctly — the failure is in how the model interpreted or applied the policy content it was given, i.e. a generation-quality issue, not an infrastructure one. The other options misdiagnose the origin: nothing in the trace suggests a tool failure (A), a network/input-corruption issue (B), or a timeout (D) — all of those would surface as errors or non-200 responses, which the trace explicitly rules out.

questions.prompt: Where should a stable instruction that must apply to every turn be placed?

options.text: At the end of the latest user message
In the system prompt
Repeated in each user message
In a tool description

questions.explanation: The system prompt is designed for persistent framing across the exchange. Placing it in user turns (A, C) mixes configuration with input, and tool descriptions (D) govern tool selection

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of over-including few-shot examples?

options.text: The API will reject the request
Token cost, and risk of the model overfitting to the examples' surface pattern rather than the underlying task
Few-shot examples are deprecated
There is no risk

questions.explanation: Extra examples cost tokens and can lock the model onto the surface pattern. They are not deprecated. The API will not reject them for being numerous in ordinary cases.

questions.prompt: A team notices a smaller, cheaper model fails to match a required output structure zero-shot, while a larger model succeeds zero-shot. What cost-conscious approach does the module suggest?

options.text: Always use the larger model, since prompting cannot compensate for capability differences.
Fine-tune the smaller model on the required structure.
Raise the smaller model's temperature until the structure appears.
Add a few worked examples to the smaller model's prompt — examples can let a cheaper model do the job — and keep the simplest model-and-examples combination that meets the eval.

questions.explanation: Prompting mode and model choice are related levers: adding a few examples can let a cheaper model match a structure a larger model gets zero-shot. Try the simplest model and fewest examples that meet the eval.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team needs a loan-underwriting assistant to follow a specific, somewhat unusual output format that's hard to describe in words alone. What is the most effective prompting technique to reliably steer this?

options.text: Describe the format abstractly in a single adjective, like 'professional.'
Provide a few concrete input/output examples (few-shot) demonstrating the exact desired format.
Ask Claude to guess the format based on the user's tone alone.
Avoid giving any examples so Claude isn't 'biased' toward a particular format.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples that concretely demonstrate the desired input/output format are typically the most effective way to steer an unusual or hard-to-describe format.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team needs a returns-processing assistant to follow a specific, somewhat unusual output format that's hard to describe in words alone. What is the most effective prompting technique to reliably steer this?

options.text: Ask Claude to guess the format based on the user's tone alone.
Avoid giving any examples so Claude isn't 'biased' toward a particular format.
Provide a few concrete input/output examples (few-shot) demonstrating the exact desired format.
Describe the format abstractly in a single adjective, like 'professional.'

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples that concretely demonstrate the desired input/output format are typically the most effective way to steer an unusual or hard-to-describe format.

questions.prompt: A QA engineer testing a Claude-powered application sets temperature to 0, expecting completely reproducible outputs, and sends the exact same prompt to the API ten times. Nine responses are identical, but one differs by a single word. The engineer assumes this must be a bug. What is the most accurate explanation?

options.text: Setting temperature to 0 disables all randomness in token selection, so the API guarantees bit-for-bit identical output on every call, meaning any observed difference must be a defect in Anthropic's serving infrastructure that engineering should file as a bug.

Even at temperature 0, minor floating-point and infrastructure-level non-determinism (e.g., parallelized computation) can still produce small variations, so bit-for-bit identical output is not guaranteed.

Temperature is a parameter that only influences how the system prompt is interpreted before generation begins, not the token-by-token sampling process during generation, so the sampling settings couldn't be responsible for the variation seen here.

Switching to a model with a larger context window would give the model more room to consider prior tokens during decoding, which would eliminate this kind of small output variation between identical requests.

questions.explanation: Temperature 0 minimizes randomness but does not create a strict determinism guarantee, because low-level numerical and infrastructure effects can still introduce tiny variations. Option A overstates what temperature 0 guarantees; option C misdescribes what temperature controls; option D is irrelevant since context window size has nothing to do with output determinism.

questions.prompt: A developer building a latency-sensitive, low-complexity summarization feature assumes that pairing the fastest, cheapest model tier with extended/adaptive thinking enabled will always be the most efficient combination, regardless of task difficulty. Which statement best describes the actual tradeoff?

options.text: Extended/adaptive thinking is only useful on the largest, most capable model tier and has no effect elsewhere, so it should always be paired with the highest tier regardless of task complexity.

For a simple, latency-sensitive task, using the fastest and cheapest model tier without thinking enabled (or at a low effort level) is usually the better fit, since reasoning features add latency and cost that provide little benefit when deep multi-step reasoning isn't required.

Cost, latency, and output quality remain essentially unaffected by which model tier or thinking configuration is selected, so any combination of model size and thinking effort will perform interchangeably on this task.

Enabling extended thinking always reduces both latency and cost compared to leaving it disabled, because the additional reasoning tokens let the model converge on a correct answer using fewer total generation steps overall.

questions.explanation: Thinking and higher effort levels add tokens and latency that pay off on genuinely hard reasoning tasks, but for a simple summarization task they mostly add cost and delay without meaningfully improving quality, so the lean configuration is usually better. Option A's premise is false since thinking can apply across tiers, option C denies the well-documented tradeoffs entirely, and option D reverses the actual relationship — thinking generally increases latency and cost, not decreases them.

questions.prompt: When should a tool return an identifier rather than the full object?

options.text: When the object is large and the model only needs it to make a subsequent call
Never, the model needs the full object
Always, to reduce cost
Only for write operations

questions.explanation: Returning a handle keeps context free when the payload is only needed for a later call. Always returning everything (B) or nothing (C) ignores the task, and the rule is not about writes (D)

questions.prompt: Claude calls a `web_search` server-side tool. What must your application code do to handle the tool_use block?

options.text: Execute the search and send back a `tool_result`
Nothing — server-side tools execute on Anthropic's infrastructure and the result arrives inline
Approve it via a hook
Convert it to a client-side tool first

questions.explanation: Server-side tools run on Anthropic. You do not send `tool_result`. Hooks are for *your* gates, not Anthropic's search. You do not have to convert it to client-side.

questions.prompt: In a trace, the assistant turn issues two parallel tool calls: `toolu_A` (`get_weather`, city=Paris) and `toolu_B` (`get_time`, city=Paris). The next user turn returns both `tool_result` blocks, but the developer accidentally swapped the two `tool_use_id` values. The API accepts the request without error. What happens, and why?

options.text: The API rejects mismatched ids only in strict mode; enabling it would have caught the swap.

The API matches results to calls by id, not by position — both ids exist, so the request is valid, and each result is silently attributed to the wrong call; the model now reasons over a time labeled as weather and vice versa. The application must map each result to the id of the call that produced it.
The API matches results by position in the content array, so the swap is harmless as long as the order matches the calls.
The model detects the inconsistency from the content and re-requests both tools.

questions.explanation: Matching is by id, not position. Since both swapped ids exist, the request validates — and each result is silently attributed to the wrong call, a worse failure than an error. The application must bind each result to the id of the call that produced it.

questions.prompt: A CI connection trace shows: a 401 Unauthorized on the first token request; the client reading the credential as a plaintext value from `/home/jenkins/.config/mcp-credentials.json`; and a 401 again on the retry with that credential. Which fix addresses everything the trace exposes?

options.text: Rotate the API key and write the new value back into `/home/jenkins/.config/mcp-credentials.json`
Rotate the rejected key, move the credential out of the file, inject it as an environment variable in the CI pipeline runner configuration, and update the MCP configuration to reference the variable
Switch this service-account connection from API key authentication to OAuth
Increase the retry count and connection timeout so transient authentication failures resolve on their own

questions.explanation: The trace shows two stacked problems: the 401 on both attempts means the key itself is rejected and must be rotated, and the plaintext credential file at a known path is the secret-handling defect. Fix B resolves both; rotating alone writes the new key back into the same insecure file, OAuth mismatches a service-account identity model, and retries cannot fix a rejected key.  ---

questions.prompt: A CI agent runs a build pipeline and, at every step, appends the full raw output of each shell command (sometimes tens of thousands of lines) to the conversation it sends back to Claude on the next turn. After about 15 steps, the agent's responses become slower, more expensive, and occasionally lose track of the original task. What is the best way to fix this?

options.text: Increase the `max_tokens` parameter on each request, giving the model a larger output allowance so it has enough room to read through the growing volume of appended command output from prior steps.
After each step, prune or summarize command output down to the parts relevant to the next decision (e.g., errors, exit codes, key log lines) instead of keeping every full transcript.
Switch the pipeline to whichever available model offers the largest context window, and continue appending every full, unabridged command transcript from every prior step exactly as before.
Stop sending any shell command output back to Claude at all after each step, and instead let the model simply guess or assume the outcome of each command based on the instructions it was given.

questions.explanation: Pruning/summarizing superseded tool output keeps the context focused on what's actually needed for the next decision, preventing bloat and drift. Raising max_tokens affects output length, not input context size, and doesn't reduce bloat. A bigger context window only delays the problem and still wastes tokens, attention, and cost on irrelevant data. Withholding tool output entirely removes the information Claude needs to make correct decisions.

questions.prompt: A document fetched from the web contains text instructing the model to ignore prior instructions. What is the correct architecture?

options.text: Add a prompt instruction telling the model to ignore embedded instructions
Treat all fetched content as data, and enforce permissions outside the model
Filter for the phrase before processing
Use a larger model, which is less susceptible

questions.explanation: Retrieved content is untrusted input, and the durable defense is that the model's authority is limited by the surrounding system rather than by its own compliance. Prompt instructions (A), phrase filters (C), and model size (D) are all bypassable.

questions.prompt: What does "fail closed" mean in the context of a guardrail check that itself errors?

options.text: Default to allowing the action so the user isn't blocked
Default to blocking the action
Retry indefinitely
Log and ignore

questions.explanation: On guardrail failure, block. Allowing through is fail open.

questions.prompt: A user of a report-generation assistant tries to get Claude to ignore its safety guidelines by framing the request as a fictional roleplay scenario. What is the correct posture for the application to take?

options.text: Treat the fictional framing as a legitimate exception and relax safety guardrails for the roleplay.
Assume jailbreak attempts are not a real concern once a system prompt exists.
Disable logging so the attempted jailbreak isn't recorded.
Maintain the same safety guardrails regardless of framing, and add application-level checks rather than relying on the model's judgment alone.

questions.explanation: Jailbreak attempts often use reframing (roleplay, hypotheticals) to bypass guidelines — the correct posture keeps guardrails consistent regardless of framing, backed by application-level checks rather than the model alone.

questions.prompt: A healthcare intake assistant built on Claude accepts free-text messages from patients that often include names, dates of birth, and insurance ID numbers. The team wants to send conversation transcripts to a third-party analytics and logging vendor for troubleshooting, without exposing patient PII. Which approach best protects patient privacy while still enabling the vendor integration?

options.text: Add an instruction to the system prompt asking Claude to avoid including patient names, birth dates, or insurance IDs in its responses, then forward the resulting raw transcripts to the vendor unfiltered.
Run transcripts through a deterministic PII redaction/masking step that strips or tokenizes identifiers before any data leaves the trusted environment and is sent to the vendor.
Encrypt the transcripts in transit using TLS while they travel to the vendor, then deliver the full, unredacted transcript text once it reaches the vendor's systems for troubleshooting.
Add a note asking patients to avoid typing personal information such as names or insurance IDs into the chat, and continue forwarding whatever transcripts result to the vendor unchanged.

questions.explanation: Deterministic redaction applied before data leaves the trusted boundary reliably prevents PII leakage; the model's own instruction-following is probabilistic and not a guarantee (option A). Transport encryption does not stop the vendor from receiving PII once decrypted (option C), and relying on end-user behavior is not an enforceable control (option D).

questions.prompt: A team is building a coding agent that includes a delete_file tool capable of permanently removing files from a user's repository. They are concerned about the model deleting files unintentionally during an autonomous session. Which approach best mitigates this risk?

options.text: Add a strongly worded warning in the system prompt instructing Claude to think carefully and double-check with the user before ever calling delete_file, relying on the model's instruction-following to prevent accidental destructive calls.

Increase the model's decoding temperature, on the theory that a less deterministic sampling process will make Claude weigh the consequences of a destructive call more carefully before invoking delete_file.
Gate execution of delete_file behind a human-approval step (e.g., an always-ask permission policy) so a person must explicitly confirm before the harness ever executes the call.

Remove delete_file's description entirely so Claude has to infer its purpose and parameters from context alone, on the assumption that reduced documentation will make the model more hesitant to invoke it.

questions.explanation: Gating a destructive, hard-to-reverse action behind a human-approval step (e.g., an always-ask permission policy) is a technical control that actually prevents unwanted execution, not just a request the model might not follow. A system-prompt warning is unenforceable and can be ignored. Increasing temperature is irrelevant — sampling doesn't govern whether a destructive tool is called. Removing the tool's description would break correct usage entirely without providing any real safeguard against misuse.
